{{short description|Type of mathematical theorem}}
In mathematics, '''homological stability''' is any of a number of theorems asserting that the [[group cohomology|group homology]] of a series of groups <math>G_1 \subset G_2 \subset \cdots </math> is stable, i.e.,
:<math>H_i(G_n)</math>
is independent of ''n'' when ''n'' is large enough (depending on ''i''). The smallest ''n'' such that the maps <math>H_i(G_n) \to H_i(G_{n+1})</math> is an isomorphism is referred to as the ''stable range''.
The concept of homological stability was pioneered by [[Daniel Quillen]] whose proof technique has been adapted in various situations.<ref>{{cite book|last=Quillen|first= D.|author-link=Daniel Quillen|chapter=Finite generation of the groups ''K''<sub>''i''</sub> of rings of algebraic integers.|title=Algebraic K-theory, I: Higher K-theories|pages=179–198|series=Lecture Notes in Math.|volume=341|publisher=Springer|year=1973}}</ref>

==Applications==
In some cases, the homology of the group
:<math>G_\infty = \bigcup_n G_n</math>
can be computed by other means or is related to other data. For example, the [[Barratt–Priddy theorem]] relates the homology of the infinite symmetric group agrees with mapping spaces of spheres. This can also be stated as a relation between the [[plus construction]] of <math>\operatorname{BS}_\infty</math> and the [[sphere spectrum]]. In a similar vein, the homology of <math>\operatorname{GL}_\infty(R)</math> is related, via the +-construction, to the [[algebraic K-theory]] of ''R''.
